newsitem.title: NORWAY: Doctors seek ways to banish winter blues.
newsitem.headline: Doctors seek ways to banish winter blues.

text.p: Under the pitch black sky of a cold Saturday in the Arctic city of Tromsoe, about 100 doctors began their search for ways to beat an illness afflicting millions of people worldwide -- winter depression.

The two-day conference concerns a condition known as Seasonal Affective Disorder, or SAD, which some psychiatrists say devastates the lives of many unknowing sufferers and in extreme cases may lead to suicide.

Professor Norman Rosenthal, head of environmental psychiatry at the National Institute of Mental Health in Bethesda in the United States and the first to identify SAD in 1984, said there were many millions of silently suffering individuals from North America to Europe and Australia.
About 10 million Americans alone are afflicted with some form of SAD, Rosenthal told Reuters at the start of the conference.
"Europe is certainly bigger than the United States. There must be an enormous amount of suffering and lack of productivity attributable to SAD that is not being recognised," he said.

Especially prevalent in the northern hemisphere, SAD is believed to be caused by a lack of daylight and is more than just a sinking feeling of "winter blues" as the days become shorter and the cold sets in.
It is characterised by depression at the onset of late autumn and lasts until spring. Symptoms include oversleeping, lethargy, a craving for carbohydrates and weight gain, anxiety and mood swings.
"I felt total despair and emptiness without knowing why. I just didn't want to live," said Jennifer Eastwood, 44, a SAD sufferer. "It's a serious, terminal illness, not a 20th century malaise."
Eastwood spent five years diagnosed as a manic depressive after her first bout of severe winter depression at the age of 28 before hearing of the syndrome.

She now chairs the British charity SAD Association, which has 2,500 paid members and receives around 1,000 telephone calls for advice each month between September and April when sufferers are at their worst.

Treatment for SAD so far mainly has been in the form of light therapy, when a patient sits in front of a light box emitting 10 to 20 times the light of a normal light bulb for several hours each day. More effective treatments are now being sought using a combination of light and drugs.
Rosenthal, himself a mild SAD sufferer, said the meeting was a landmark in the awareness and recognition of the condition as a serious psychiatric syndrome.
"This conference represents a coming of age of SAD and shows it is worthy of special attention in order to alleviate the suffering of millions," he said.
Tromsoe, Norway's most northerly city within the Arctic Circle, provided an approriate location. Between late November and the end of January its inhabitants are shrouded in darkness 24 hours a day.
"It was a stroke of public relations genius to stage the conference here," Rosenthal said as he switched on his light box for a much needed dose of startling, white light.
"Oh man, that's too much. It feels like I'm on a drug. It's a feeling of everything is going to be just fine and there's no need to worry about anything," he laughed.
